tasks.task: Future continuous first listen, including planned part pauses
Submit first answers and confidence, without a second play
Four Q-located intensive segments, 15 minutes each

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Theatre learning office.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Hello. I'm interested in your practical workshops, but I'm unsure which one suits me. I enjoy watching performances, although I have no ambition to act.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: We offer several sessions about work behind the scenes. What would you most like to explore?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Set design. I've tried making small models at home, and I'd like to understand how a stage space develops from an idea.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Then I'll record set design as your main interest. We also run costume sessions, but those focus on a different process.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: The set session sounds right. I'm looking for an introduction rather than a professional qualification.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Which date are you considering?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I first wrote down February the fifteenth, because a friend sent me an early programme.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: That session has moved. The available date is the twenty-second of February.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: The twenty-second is fine; I just need to change the note I sent to my sister.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Please do. We will repeat the date in your confirmation, and the booking page now shows the revised programme.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I'll use that confirmation when arranging transport. I don't want us to arrive a week early simply because we both saved the same old picture without checking whether the details were final.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Is it a morning workshop?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: No, the group begins at one forty in the afternoon. The building opens earlier for other activities, but your session starts at one forty.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I'll put the afternoon time in my calendar. I had assumed it began just after lunch at one, so I'm glad I asked.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: You can arrive a little before the start and check in at the learning desk.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: That's helpful. My sister prefers to leave some spare time for finding the entrance, and we won't assume that an open building means the workshop leader is ready to start before the booked time.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: How many places would you like?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: There are four people in our informal art group, but one has a work commitment that day. Could I book three places?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Three places are available.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Good. The fourth person may ask about another date, but I shouldn't reserve a seat just in case.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Exactly. You can send them the public information sheet, and they can contact us separately. If somebody in your booking later drops out, tell us rather than arranging an informal replacement. We need to know who is attending so the leader can prepare the right number of work areas and introductory materials.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: How much does the group booking cost?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: For the three introductory places, the total is forty-five pounds.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Is that forty-five pounds each?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: No, forty-five for the booking as a whole. Specialist follow-up workshops have different prices, so please make sure you're looking at the introduction when you check the website.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I will. We have a small shared budget and need a clear total before paying.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Your confirmation will show the number of places and the total together. If either differs from what we've discussed, contact the office so that we can correct it before you complete the payment.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Should we bring our own modelling tools?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: We supply the tools and materials for the exercise. Please bring an apron, because some of the materials can mark clothing.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I have an apron from a painting class. I'll bring the apron and tell the others to do the same.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Good. You don't need to buy equipment for this introduction. A notebook is optional if you like making written notes, but the apron is the practical item we ask everyone to bring.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: That keeps the preparation simple. I'd rather try the process first than purchase tools before discovering which part of it interests me.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Do we need drawing experience? My sister worries that her sketches aren't good enough to show other people.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: The workshop is designed for beginners. The leader uses simple exercises to explore space and explain choices, rather than judging polished drawings.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: So previous drawing skill isn't an entry requirement?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: That's right. Participants can use rough shapes and explain what they intend. A useful model doesn't have to look like a finished exhibition object.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I'll pass that on. She enjoys thinking about how a room works but wouldn't come if she thought everyone had to compete to produce the most impressive artwork by the end.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Will we be able to watch the rehearsal afterwards?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Only if a separate public rehearsal event is scheduled and you book that event. The workshop does not include access to ordinary company rehearsals.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I wondered because the activities take place in the same building.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: They do, but different spaces have different access arrangements. The workshop leader may use a prepared example from a production, which isn't the same as inviting the group into a live rehearsal.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Understood. We'll plan around the workshop itself and check the public programme if we want to add another activity, rather than assume that one booking opens every room.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: One of us may need to sit for much of the session. Should we wait until the day to discuss that?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Please tell us in your reply to the confirmation. The leader can explain how the activity is organised and consider an appropriate work position. We shouldn't promise a solution without understanding the practical requirement.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I'll describe it in advance and ask what is available.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Thank you. That gives us time to discuss any limits as well as the possibilities.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: It also means the person can decide with clear information, instead of arriving and feeling obliged to attempt an arrangement that doesn't work for them.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: If the workshop moves to another room, how will we know?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: We'll send a direct booking update and put a notice at the learning desk. Please follow the revised message, even if your original confirmation shows a different room.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Should we use the main theatre entrance shown on old posters?

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Use the entrance in the current booking instructions. Some posters advertise performances rather than learning sessions.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I'll keep the final message accessible on my phone and share it with the other two participants.

turns.speaker: Coordinator
turns.text: Excellent. A shared current version is more useful than several screenshots from different stages of the programme.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: Welcome to the theatre's learning spaces. The diagram has north at the top and the entrance on the southern edge. The central foyer is our fixed reference point. Eight lettered areas surround it, and the letters are locations rather than the initials of room names. The costume workshop is directly west of the foyer, level with its centre. It is not in the north-west corner. We use that room for demonstrations and supervised practical sessions. Please wait outside until the leader invites your group in, even if another activity appears to have finished. The team may still be counting equipment or preparing materials for the next session.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: The prop display is in the north-east corner. An earlier programme placed it in the north-west area, but the display moved when we reorganised the learning programme. On today's diagram it is above and to the right of the foyer. It also lies east of the northern central studio, since both rooms are on the same northern row. The display includes objects prepared for teaching rather than items visitors can borrow. Ask before touching anything, even if it looks like an ordinary household object. A familiar appearance doesn't tell you how something has been made or whether it is intended to be handled during this particular session.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: The main learning studio is directly north of the foyer. It is west of the prop display, not south-west of it, because the two areas sit on the same northern row of this schematic map. Your set-design workshop will begin in that studio today. There is enough table space for small groups to arrange materials and compare their ideas. Please keep personal bags away from the working surfaces unless the leader asks you to take something out. We want everyone to be able to see the example and reach their own materials. The room is a shared learning space, so leave it ready for the group that follows yours.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: Completed workshop models are collected from the collection point in the south-east area. That is below and to the right of the foyer, and south of the room directly east of the foyer. The collection point is separate from the entrance desk, even if both have staff nearby. Before taking a model away, check its label with the team so that similar-looking work doesn't become mixed up. If an item needs time to dry, staff will explain the available arrangement. Don't assume that leaving it on a studio table guarantees somebody will know which group it belongs to or when you intend to return for it.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: The break area is in the south-west corner, west of the room directly south of the foyer. It is on the opposite side of the map from the collection point. Visitors can sit there between scheduled activities, but it isn't a room reserved exclusively for one workshop. Please leave space for other groups and take personal belongings when you move on. The break area isn't the place to store unfinished models, which should remain within the leader's agreed arrangement. On your map, identify the south-west letter for this final location. You now have the costume workshop, prop display, studio, collection point and break area marked for today's visit.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: During a practical task, the leader may ask groups to stop working and compare two approaches. Those pauses are part of the learning process. They allow participants to explain why a choice was made, see its consequences and consider another possibility. The aim isn't to identify the fastest group or rank the models by appearance. A model that exposes a problem can be useful if the group can explain what it learned. Please resist the temptation to hide an unfinished attempt whenever discussion begins. The conversation concerns the development of an idea, and sometimes an abandoned version shows that development more clearly than the neat final version alone.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: You may photograph your own work, but a close photograph that includes another participant or their work should be discussed with them first under the workshop arrangements. A picture taken for personal reference isn't automatically suitable for the theatre's public publicity. The team uses a separate process when collecting contributions for that purpose. If someone prefers not to be included, adjust the photograph rather than treating their presence in a group activity as agreement. You can usually show the learning point by changing the angle or photographing your own model later. Ask the leader if you're unsure which arrangement applies to a particular use.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: Some materials are shared between tables. When you need an item, use the collection and return process the leader demonstrates. Taking it from another group's active workspace can interrupt their task and make the stock record unreliable. If a shared item isn't available, tell the leader; another approach may work for the exercise. The point is to explore a design problem with the resources provided, not to make every group use identical materials at the same instant. Returning an item promptly gives other participants a fair opportunity to try it. Please also report a damaged item rather than placing it back where the next person may mistake it for a usable one.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: At the end of the task, groups will describe one change they made and the reason for it. That explanation should connect the initial idea, the problem noticed and the revised choice. Saying that the second version looked better gives little information about the decision. You might instead explain that moving a doorway made a route clearer, or that reducing the model's height improved visibility from another position. These are examples of the kind of reasoning requested, not instructions to make a particular design change. Different groups may retain different solutions, provided they can explain how their choices respond to the problem they were trying to solve.

turns.speaker: Learning host
turns.text: Please complete the short feedback form after the workshop. It asks about the clarity of the task and whether you had an opportunity to participate. It doesn't ask you to compare your artistic ability with another participant's. If an instruction was confusing, name the stage where the confusion arose and describe what you expected to happen. That helps the team distinguish a wording problem from a missing demonstration or a practical arrangement that needs attention. You can also identify something that helped you learn. A useful review considers what to retain as well as what to change, instead of assuming improvement requires replacing every feature of the session.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: For your visitor-flow pilot, should the first task be deliberately simple?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: Yes. Asking people to find the learning desk would let them become familiar with the task format.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I was worried that an easy task wouldn't produce useful data, but its purpose is preparation. I support using it first if we keep those results separate.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: So you wouldn't treat successful completion as proof that the whole building is easy to navigate?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: Exactly. It's a way to check that people understand what we're asking them to do. Then the later task can focus on a less obvious destination without also testing whether the participant understands the procedure.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Clara suggests allowing anonymous written feedback after the route task.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: I favour it. Somebody might mention a confusing moment they don't want to discuss face to face.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I'd prefer a short conversation linked to the observation record. Anonymous comments could be difficult to interpret without knowing which route the person took.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: We could ask them to indicate the route version without giving a name.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: That helps, but I still prefer the conversation for this pilot.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Does your proposal remain, Clara?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: Yes. I think an anonymous option is worth including, even if we can't connect every comment to an individual observed action.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Your first draft proposes charging participants a small admission fee.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I thought it might discourage people from agreeing and then failing to attend.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: I don't support a fee for a student study. It could change who volunteers, and we aren't offering a separate paid event.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: You're right. After reading the project brief, I no longer think charging is appropriate.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What will you do instead?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Send a reminder and make it easy for someone to withdraw.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: That seems practical.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I'll remove the fee from the draft entirely. It isn't a proposal I'm keeping in reserve for a later stage of this same pilot.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Where should the observer stand?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I support a fixed position beside the foyer corner. It provides a view of the junction without requiring us to follow participants closely.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: I'd use two observers who can cover different parts of the route. A single corner won't show where a person goes after leaving the foyer.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: That's true, but the pilot question concerns the decision at this junction. I still favour the fixed corner position.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Clara, does narrowing the question resolve your concern?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: It clarifies the claim, but I still prefer two positions because a return from the wrong corridor would be informative. We haven't reached agreement on the arrangement.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Will you review the procedure halfway through the pilot?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: Yes, we should check whether the observation categories are working before using them for all the remaining sessions.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I agree, provided we record any revisions and don't silently combine unlike categories.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What might trigger a revision?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: A situation that both observers see but consistently classify differently.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Or a category that requires us to infer an intention we cannot actually observe.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: Then we both support a midpoint review, with a clear record of what changes.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. A review can improve the method, but it also creates a boundary that the later analysis needs to acknowledge.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Should the revised route task be tested with the same participant group?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: I'd bring the same group back for one limited check. They can compare the instructions directly and identify what became clearer.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I'd recruit new people. The returning group may remember the destination, so it would be difficult to tell whether the revision helped them find it.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: I accept that we couldn't use their speed as a clean comparison. I still support asking them back to discuss the wording.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Dev?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: For our next session, I remain in favour of new participants. We could invite separate comments from the original group later if time permits.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Which two measures have you agreed to collect at the learning desk?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: First, the length of the queue at our scheduled observation points.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: Yes, under a rule that distinguishes people waiting for help from people standing nearby talking.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Would you collect the names of everyone in the queue?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: No. Names don't help answer this question.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: We also rejected recording what each visitor bought at the theatre shop. That might interest another project, but it isn't a measure of the desk's information process.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then the queue count is your first agreed measure, with the definition written down before you start observing.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What is the second agreed measure?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: Count interruptions to the desk worker's current explanation. For example, another visitor may ask a question before the first explanation is finished.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Agreed. We'll define observable interruptions and avoid guessing whether they were irritating.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you measuring the age of every visitor as well?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: No, that isn't one of the selected measures.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: Nor are we estimating people's income from their appearance.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. The two measures are the queue length at scheduled checks and interruptions to explanations. They describe parts of the process, although neither alone tells you whether visitors eventually understood the information they received.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Suppose the queue is shorter in the second session. Which two changes prevent a simple claim that the new sign caused the improvement?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: The route into the foyer changed between sessions. That could change how many people reached the desk, independently of the sign.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Yes. We need to state that limitation.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Is using the same observation sheet itself a problem?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: No; keeping the method consistent helps.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: And recording the session date isn't a weakness either.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Exactly. You are looking for competing explanations of the changed queue, not treating every feature of the observation process as a reason to reject the study.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What is the other relevant change?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: A different member of staff worked at the desk in the second session. Their way of answering questions might affect how quickly the queue moved.

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: Agreed. With both the route and the staff member changing, we can't isolate the effect of the sign from this comparison alone.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Does that mean you should hide the shorter queue?

turns.speaker: Clara
turns.text: No, report it as an observation and explain what the design cannot establish.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: The sessions did take place, so cancellation isn't a limitation.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. Keep the result and the causal claim separate, then propose a next stage that can examine the alternatives more carefully.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Consider a fictional community programme that offers introductory creative workshops. Before collecting results, the evaluation team defines an outcome. An outcome is the change the programme hopes to support, rather than merely the activity it delivers. For this example, the team focuses on participants' ability to explain one design decision using evidence from their own work. Counting sessions is useful for describing delivery, but it doesn't measure that particular ability. A clear outcome guides the task used to gather evidence and prevents the team from replacing a difficult question with an easier count after the programme has finished. It also helps explain what the evaluation deliberately leaves outside its scope.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The second stage establishes a baseline before participants begin the programme. The baseline is a starting measure taken with a task appropriate to the chosen outcome. It should not require knowledge that the introductory programme never intends to address. Nor should it be so different from the later task that any change becomes impossible to interpret. In this example, participants describe a choice in a simple prepared model. The team records the response using a stated method. A baseline doesn't explain why participants differ, but it provides a reference for describing what changes within the observed group during the period covered by the evaluation.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The third stage selects a comparison that suits the question and acknowledges the available constraints. A simple before-and-after comparison can describe change, but it doesn't automatically establish what caused that change. Participants may have practised elsewhere or encountered other relevant experiences during the same period. If another group is used for comparison, the team needs to consider how that group was selected and whether its circumstances are genuinely comparable. Merely giving the groups different names does not solve those problems. The comparison is part of the reasoning, and its limits should be explained before the final results encourage readers to treat every difference as a programme effect.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fourth stage records attendance during the programme. Attendance helps the team describe which activities each participant actually encountered. Someone booked for four sessions may attend only one, while another person attends every session but misses the final evaluation. Those are different records, and the team should not turn a booking into proof of participation. The attendance record also helps identify practical obstacles that might deserve investigation. It cannot by itself tell researchers how engaged a person was or what they learned. In this example it provides context for interpretation, rather than a substitute for the task that measures the chosen outcome.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fifth stage gathers follow-up evidence after the final workshop. The follow-up uses the agreed task and records who was available to complete it. The team keeps the timing visible because a response collected immediately afterwards may differ from one collected several weeks later. If circumstances force a change to the schedule, that change is documented rather than hidden inside a single final column. The purpose is to maintain a clear relationship between the evaluation plan and what actually happened. A tidy table is helpful only when readers can understand the observations represented by its entries, including the occasions when planned evidence could not be collected.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: One question concerns displacement. If participants would have attended another similar workshop without this programme, some activity may have shifted from one provider to another rather than being entirely new. This possibility doesn't mean the programme has no value. It means that a claim about creating additional participation needs more support than a count of people attending. The team may ask carefully framed questions about alternatives, while recognising that answers about hypothetical choices have limits. Reporting displacement as a possibility is different from assuming that every participant would definitely have done the same thing elsewhere. The evaluation should make the uncertainty visible instead of choosing whichever story produces the strongest headline.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Selection also matters. People who volunteer for a creative programme may already be interested in the subject or have more time available than those who do not join. If participants later perform differently from non-participants, those initial differences could contribute to the result. The team should examine what it knows about recruitment and starting circumstances rather than assuming that the programme is the only difference between the groups. This is especially important when a small pilot relies on people who respond to an enthusiastic invitation. The pilot can still provide useful information, but the invitation and resulting sample belong in the explanation of what that information can support.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Another issue is attrition, meaning that some participants are missing from the follow-up. If people who found the programme less useful are less likely to respond, the available feedback may present a more favourable picture than the experience of the whole starting group. The team should report how many people were invited and how many provided evidence, without inventing responses for those who did not. It can describe what is known about the missing cases and what remains uncertain. Treating every missing response as failure would be unjustified, but treating the remaining respondents as a complete account of the original group would also conceal an important limitation.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Costs deserve a clear description alongside outcomes. The evaluation may count materials and staff time, but it should also explain the boundary used for that count. A room provided without a direct charge still represents a resource someone made available. Whether and how that resource enters the calculation depends on the stated question. The team should avoid comparing one programme's narrow cash total with another programme's much broader resource estimate as though the figures meant the same thing. A consistent account of costs helps readers assess practical choices. It doesn't reduce every benefit to money or imply that the cheapest activity is automatically the best one.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: At the stage review, the team lists unresolved questions for the next trial. These open questions might concern the comparison group, the follow-up interval or a task that participants interpreted differently from the researchers. The review should connect each proposed change to the difficulty it is intended to address. Adding more questions to a form isn't necessarily an improvement if the original problem was unclear wording or missing contact arrangements. The team also records which features worked well enough to retain. The next trial then becomes a purposeful revision of the method, with reasons that another person can examine, rather than a new version whose changes are impossible to trace back to evidence.
